segments.text: Groww is India’s number one stockbroker today. Out of every three new SIPs, one is created through Groww.
But surprisingly, this multi-thousand-crore company was built by the son of a farmer, who came from a village that didn’t even have an English-medium school.
At just seven years old, he had to live away from his parents. Lalit Keshre was born in a village called Lepa in Madhya Pradesh.
The village was so underdeveloped that his parents had to send him to Khargone city to get a better education. He stayed with his maternal grandparents there.
Luckily, that same year, the first English-medium school opened in Khargone, and Lalit became its forty-second student.
He was an average student, but somehow he topped his class in the second grade. After this, his grandfather praised him with just one word: “Good", only good.
But that one word inspired him throughout his life to always strive for excellence. Years later, while in school, Lalit spotted a thick book in the library.
The principal told him that it was for IIT-JEE preparation — one of the toughest exams in India.
Until that day, neither Lalit nor any of his classmates had even heard of IIT.
But because the principal described it as a “complicated exam,” Lalit decided that was exactly what he wanted to prepare for.
He subscribed to the postal-based coaching program of Brilliant Tutorials. Every month, he received study materials delivered by post.
He prepared day and night, completely by himself. He took the exam and got selected for IIT Bombay in Microelectronics Engineering.
At IIT, while other students focused only on campus life, placements, and grades, Lalit’s approach to life was different.
Because of pollen on campus, he often suffered from allergies.
So he applied his engineering knowledge practically and created an allergen detector device that warned him in advance about allergens in the environment.
This proved that he already had a passion for problem-solving and entrepreneurship. Apart from this, IIT gave Lalit exposure to the stock market.
He started watching financial news, tracking capital markets, and even bought a share worth ₹80 using his scholarship money.
Back then, opening a stock market account meant standing in long lines, filling out physical paperwork, and paying high brokerage fees.
But Lalit had no idea that one day, he would solve this exact problem for the entire country.
After graduating from IIT, Lalit joined Ittiam Systems. It was an Indian company that built video-streaming software or clients like Google and Netflix,
ensuring videos could reach users without delay. Working there, Lalit realised the power of video content.
He remembered how, in childhood, he had to live away from his parents just to get a good education, and even for IIT, he had prepared without any guidance.
So in 2011, he started Eduflix — basically, a Netflix for education.
The idea was to bring India’s best teachers online and deliver quality education across the country through live streaming.
Surprisingly, Lalit came up with this idea years before Unacademy, BYJU’S, or PW. But ironically, that very fact also became the reason Eduflix failed.
At that time, India’s infrastructure wasn’t advanced enough to support large-scale video streaming. Nor did every household have a laptop or smartphone.
So after nearly three years of effort, Eduflix shut down. But this failure taught Lalit a massive business lesson:
“Timing is everything in a startup.” After this crushing failure, Lalit decided to join India’s biggest startup — Flipkart.
While working there, an incident occurred during Raksha Bandhan. Due to a technical error, many Rakhi orders were cancelled.
Flipkart could have just sent an apology email and closed the matter. But that night, 10–15 engineers stayed back in the office,
packed Rakhis themselves, and ensured customers received them on the day of Raksha Bandhan.
This incident taught Lalit how important customer obsession is for building a successful business. He also observed that the faster the delivery,
the higher the customer satisfaction.
That’s when he thought — not of three-day, two-day, or one-day delivery — but one-hour delivery.
He even ran a pilot project called Flipkart Quick. Basically, the same concept that Zepto, Swiggy, and Blinkit are using today, Lalit had already piloted in 2015.
But again, due to a lack of infrastructure, the idea couldn’t scale up then. Flipkart was a fantastic place to work, but Lalit had bigger dreams.
He wanted to build a startup that would be as impactful as Flipkart. His only goal now was to choose co-founders who were better than himself.
Soon, Harsh Jain, Neeraj Singh, and Ishan Bansal joined him — all three were working at Flipkart at the time.
Once the team was formed, it was time to come up with a startup idea. Every Sunday, they began meeting for breakfast.
Surprisingly, they found themselves talking about the same thing every time — the stock market and investing.
They kept asking: Why is opening a Demat account so painful? Why are mutual funds so complicated?
And why are only 2 crore Indians investing in mutual funds when 20 crore have the money to do so?
Around this time, India was witnessing the Digital India initiative, Aadhaar-enabled eKYC, and the entry of Jio.
That meant, unlike Eduflix and Flipkart Quick, this time the infrastructure was ready. So they decided to build a startup in the financial services space.
Before moving forward, they made an important announcement:
we are hiring talented freelance researchers and video editors who can take our content to the next level.
Anyone interested could apply by sending an email to the given address. In the email, cover these three things: Why do you want to work with us?
How can you help our channel grow? And what is your past work experience (with work samples attached)?
Professionalism, tone, and writing style matter a lot. That's why download QuillBot’s Chrome extension before writing,
as it catches grammar, punctuation, and spelling mistakes in real-time and fixes them with one click. Its paraphrasing feature is a game-changer.
It helps to transform messages into formal, fluent, or creative styles.
Plus, its AI customisation makes it adaptable to different writing contexts. And QuillBot extension isn't limited to emails.
It works everywhere you write online: LinkedIn, Twitter, Google Docs, anywhere.
Basically, QuillBot helps you write clearly and professionally across emails, social media captions, YouTube scripts, and project reports.
The link to the extension and my email ID are both in the pinned comment and description. Now, coming back to the video. Finally, in 2017, they launched Groww,
a platform that would revolutionise simplicity in investing.
Initially, they launched only a website because they didn’t have the funds to build an app. The Groww website only offered mutual funds.
It provided all the information such as fund manager profiles, expense ratios, performance over the last 1, 3, 5, and 10 years, and risk ratings.
Users could check all this data and make their own investment decisions.
They thought, “If we get even 100 users in the first month, we’ll continue.” But in the very first month, 600 users joined without any paid marketing.
This small success was a huge achievement for the founders. They felt charged up. Month after month, Groww kept adding new users.
Meanwhile, co-founder and CTO Neeraj Singh built the Groww app, and finally, they received funding from renowned investors.
Groww had found its product-market fit. Now, it was time to scale this proven concept across India.
But Groww wasn’t alone in the market. Players like Zerodha, Upstox, and 5paisa were already offering discount broking services.
To compete, Groww had to do something unique. They noticed one common thing among competitors:
all were focused on direct stock investing and trading because that’s where the revenue potential was highest.
So Groww decided to do the exact opposite. They started with extremely simple products,
where even beginners could easily invest — mutual funds.
They also made another bold decision to completely stop offering regular mutual funds and offer only direct ones.
Regular funds charged users 1 to 1.5% extra commission, which the platform kept.
But Groww, thinking of customer benefit, made its commission completely zero. As a result, from 2017 to 2021,
Groww had almost no meaningful revenue for four years. But during that time, they built a base of nearly 2 crore registered users who trusted Groww.
So when they finally launched stock trading, 1.8 lakh Demat accounts were opened on day one.
Groww charged zero account-opening fees and zero annual maintenance charges, while competitors still charged both.
Instead, Groww charged brokerage only on buy/sell transactions because the focus was still not revenue, but trust.
One by one, new products were launched: ETFs, IPOs, intraday trading, F&O, and more.
The platform that started as a mutual fund service now had the vision to offer every kind of financial service.
When they launched stock trading and began monetising, their revenue exploded from ₹52.7 crore in FY21 to ₹4062 crore in FY25,
about 77 times growth in just four years. But success doesn’t come merely from launching multiple products.
The real secret behind their success was customer obsession.
Even today, CEO Lalit Keshre personally uses the Groww app for two hours daily and interacts directly with customers to gain the same perspective as the users.
Every employee, whether engineer, designer, or even Lalit himself, regularly works in customer support to understand real user problems.
If a user faces issues in eKYC or doesn’t understand the process, Groww’s customer support executives personally visit their homes to collect signatures.
But they took customer obsession to an entirely new level in 2023. SEBI released a report showing that 9 out of 10 people trading in F&O were losing money,
meaning 90% of them were failing. So Groww introduced features that benefited users,
even if it meant revenue loss for the company. If a user continuously incurred losses, Groww automatically blocked their trading,
depending on loss amount and income level. If the market was too volatile, Groww allowed users to pause F&O trading.
And if users exceeded their safe limit, they received warnings. This showed that Groww’s focus was on building long-term loyal customers.
When users saw that Groww’s features helped them reduce losses and genuinely build wealth, they stuck with the platform.
The longer users invested through Groww, the more chances Groww had to earn revenue. As a result of this customer obsession,
70–80% of Groww’s users today join the platform purely through word of mouth. Finally, looking at Groww’s marketing strategy, it doesn’t even feel like marketing.
They completely flipped the traditional marketing model. While competitors spent crores on TV ads, celebrity endorsements, and influencer marketing,
Groww focused entirely on education. Today, they run 19 educational YouTube channels.
Their main channel has 2.4 million subscribers,
plus seven regional-language channels — Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Gujarati, and Bengali,
helping them reach non-English-speaking Tier 2 and Tier 3 audiences.
They’ve also launched specialised channels like Mutual Funds by Groww, IPO Review by Groww, and Money Talks by Groww for personal finance.
On the internet, they’ve created over 60,000 educational pages, which mainly of three types: educational articles,
thousands of individual stock pages with real-time data, and over 200 calculators.
So when someone searches “What is a mutual fund,” “TCS share price,” or “SIP calculator,” Groww’s web page appears on the first page of the search engine thanks to brilliant SEO.
As a result, millions visit Groww’s website every month, get educated, and eventually start trusting the platform.
But they knew digital marketing alone wouldn’t suffice. So in 2020, they launched the “Ab India Karega Invest” campaign.
They toured over 250 cities — 60% of them Tier 2 and Tier 3
— conducting free workshops and conferences with industry experts to teach people how to invest through Groww.
What are mutual funds? How do SIPs work? How to manage risk? etc. Essentially, Groww replaced marketing with education.
When millions of users learned the basics of investing and personal finance from Groww for the first time, they built immense trust in the brand.
So when they finally decided to start investing, they naturally chose Groww. Of course, today, for brand awareness,
Groww has also started investing in TV ads, cricket sponsorships, and influencer marketing.
But if you notice, every one of Groww’s marketing strategies had one main goal -- to win the customer’s trust.
Even if some marketing decisions didn’t look practical on paper due to low immediate ROI,
the brand name and logo reached millions of Indians, building credibility that would pay off for years to come.
In one interview, Lalit Keshre said he isn’t building this company for today or next year, but for the coming decades.
And because of this long-term vision, Groww’s growth continues to compound every year. Today, it operates across 98% of India’s pin codes.
With around 27% market share, it is India’s number one stockbroker.
But the most remarkable thing is that Groww achieved all this not by exploiting customers, but by educating them. This was the story of Groww.
